description: LunarXplorer is a six-member student team from Grades 7–9 developing an interactive lunar landing-site navigator focused on the Moon’s south polar region. Using NASA datasets, including LRO/LOLA and LROC terrain products, we investigate elevation, slope, illumination and surface hazards to evaluate potential landing areas. Our goal is to make lunar exploration and landing-site assessment more visual, scientific and accessible.
summary: We developed Lunar Landing Planner, an interactive 3D web app that helps students and mission planners explore the Moon and judge landing conditions, with a focus on the south pole. Using NASA LRO imagery, users rotate the Moon, pick any point and date, and see Sun elevation, Earth visibility, power, communication and estimated temperature. It also offers a rover view, a Mission Design planner and a South Pole Mission Lab. This addresses the challenge by combining scattered lunar data ideas into one clear tool. It matters because light and line-of-sight decide whether a lunar mission can work, and because every result is labelled preliminary, so it teaches careful, evidence-based planning.
details:
LUNARxPLORERS BY SGS – Exploring and Planning a Landing on the Moon

We are a team of five students from Grades 8 and 9. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we developed LUNARxPLORERS BY SGS, an interactive platform that helps people explore the Moon and understand how scientists study possible landing locations.

1. What does our project do?

We know that landing on the Moon is not easy. Astronauts and spacecraft need a suitable place to land. The landing location should have enough sunlight to generate power, a clear communication path to Earth and a surface that can be studied for possible hazards.

Our project brings these ideas together in one interactive website.

Users can:

  • Explore a rotating 3D model of the Moon.
  • Zoom in and explore craters, lunar regions and landing locations.
  • Select a location and view its latitude and longitude.
  • Study sunlight and check whether Earth is visible from the selected location.
  • Explore estimated temperature and local lunar time.
  • Experience a simulated rover journey on the lunar surface.
  • Compare different landing locations using our Mission Science Lab and South Pole Mission Lab.
  • Generate a mission report and explore different mission-planning tools.

2. How does it work?

We developed our project as a website. When users open it, they can start their lunar exploration journey by entering the interactive Moon environment.

They can select a location on the Moon and choose a date and time. The application uses calculations and simplified models to show the Sun's position, Earth visibility and other landing conditions.

We also created mission labs where users can explore different landing scenarios, compare locations and understand the factors that scientists consider before planning a lunar landing.

3. What benefits does it have?

Through this project, we want to make learning about the Moon more interesting and practical.

Our platform can help students:

  • Understand why choosing a lunar landing location is difficult.
  • Learn about the Moon's craters, surface and geography.
  • Understand why sunlight is important for spacecraft power.
  • Learn why communication between Earth and a lunar lander is important.
  • Explore how mathematics, science and computer programming are used in space missions.

4. What tools and technologies did we use?

We used the following technologies to build our project:

  • HTML – to create the structure of our website.
  • CSS – to design the website and its different sections.
  • JavaScript – to make the website interactive and perform calculations.
  • WebGL – to display the interactive 3D Moon.
  • NASA LRO and LROC resources – to study lunar images and surface features.
  • NASA Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap – to explore lunar maps and research resources.

5. What makes our project creative?

We did not want to make just another website showing facts about the Moon. We wanted users to feel like they were taking part in a lunar mission.

That is why we created an experience that starts with exploring the Moon from space and then moves towards studying the lunar surface. We also included a rover simulation, mission labs, location comparisons and mission reports.

We tried to bring different parts of lunar exploration into one platform.

6. What factors did we consider?

While developing the project, we learned that a landing location must be studied carefully. We considered:

  • Sunlight availability for generating power.
  • Earth visibility for communication.
  • Nearby craters and possible surface hazards.
  • Estimated surface temperature.
  • Location and lunar coordinates.
  • The importance of studying terrain before landing.

7. What did we learn?

This project helped us understand that space missions need more than rockets and astronauts. Scientists and engineers must study the environment, collect information, perform calculations and make careful decisions.

We also learned how HTML, CSS, JavaScript, 3D visualization and scientific information can be combined to create an interactive application.

Our project is an educational prototype. Some terrain, rover and landing assessments are simplified simulations and are not suitable for actual spacecraft landing decisions. We hope to improve it in the future by adding more detailed lunar elevation, slope, surface hazard and sunlight datasets.

Our goal is simple: to explore the Moon, understand its challenges and learn how future explorers can prepare for a safe landing.
